Let’s cut through the licensing maze first

A financial services client we worked with last year, about 850 seats, spent three months going back and forth with their Microsoft reseller trying to figure out which Defender plan they actually needed. They had already paid for Plan 1 bundled inside Microsoft 365 Business Premium, assumed that was “enough,” and then got hit with a lateral movement incident their tooling simply didn’t catch in time. Attacker dwell time: 11 days.

Plan 1 has no EDR. That’s the short explanation for what went wrong.

So this article is aimed at the people making that decision, security architects, IT directors, whoever owns the endpoint security budget, who need a clear picture of what each Defender tier actually does, what it costs in 2026, and where the real gaps are. No vendor positioning. Just the breakdown, including some things Microsoft’s own documentation buries.

What the three tiers actually are (and where people get confused)

Microsoft has done a genuinely impressive job of confusing its own customers with naming. “Microsoft Defender for Endpoint” is the product. Inside that product there are two plans. Then there’s “Microsoft Defender XDR,” which is a suite wrapping Defender for Endpoint Plan 2 together with Defender for Office 365, Defender for Identity, Defender for Cloud Apps, and a unified portal experience. These are not interchangeable terms, and the confusion costs organizations real money at renewal time.

Plan 1 is basically next-gen antivirus plus attack surface reduction rules. It’s what you get bundled with Microsoft 365 E3, Business Premium, and a handful of other SKUs. Device discovery, web content filtering, controlled folder access. That’s genuinely useful for baseline hygiene, but this is not an EDR product. You cannot do behavioral analysis, timeline investigations, or automated response with Plan 1 alone. Full stop.

Plan 2 is where Defender for Endpoint becomes an actual EDR platform. You get the device timeline, threat hunting via advanced hunting queries (KQL-based), automated investigation and response (AIR), behavioral sensors for endpoint detection, and access to the Microsoft Defender Vulnerability Management add-on capability. One thing that catches people off guard: server licensing for Windows Server and Linux runs through Defender for Servers inside Microsoft Defender for Cloud, billed separately through Azure. It does not come with your endpoint license.

XDR is the full cross-workload picture. Incidents pull correlated signals from endpoints, email, identity, and cloud apps into one queue. If you’re running a SOC, or trying to run one without tripling headcount, that signal correlation alone is worth real money in analyst time saved. We’ll get into the specifics below.

Feature comparison: what you actually get at each tier

Capability Defender for Endpoint Plan 1 Defender for Endpoint Plan 2 Microsoft Defender XDR
Next-gen antivirus (NGAV) Yes Yes Yes
Attack surface reduction rules Yes Yes Yes
Device discovery Yes Yes Yes
Web content filtering Yes Yes Yes
Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR) No Yes Yes
Device timeline and forensics No Yes Yes
Automated Investigation and Response (AIR) No Yes Yes
Advanced threat hunting (KQL) No Yes Yes
Threat and vulnerability management (core) No Yes Yes
Microsoft Defender Vulnerability Management add-on No Partial (add-on available) Add-on available
Deception techniques (decoy assets) No No (add-on) No (add-on)
Server support No Via Defender for Servers (separate billing) Via Defender for Servers (separate billing)
Cross-workload XDR correlation (email, identity, cloud) No No Yes
Unified incident queue across workloads No No Yes
Microsoft Secure Score Limited Yes Yes (full suite)

A few things the table above doesn’t fully capture. The vulnerability management piece is worth unpacking because Microsoft has split it into two distinct layers. Core TVM, meaning software inventory, CVE exposure, and remediation task tracking, ships with Plan 2. The premium add-on, formally “Microsoft Defender Vulnerability Management,” adds browser extension inventory, certificate assessment, network share analysis, and authenticated scan capabilities for network devices. That add-on runs roughly $2 USD per user per month on top of whatever base plan you’re running. Microsoft’s official documentation breaks down what’s in core versus the add-on if you want the granular list.

Pricing in 2026: what Microsoft publishes vs. what you pay

Published list prices as of early 2026, pulled from Microsoft’s product page and the Microsoft 365 licensing guide:

Plan / SKU Standalone list price (per user/month) Typically included in
Defender for Endpoint Plan 1 ~$3.00 USD Microsoft 365 E3, Business Premium, A3
Defender for Endpoint Plan 2 ~$5.20 USD (standalone add-on) Microsoft 365 E5, E5 Security
Microsoft 365 E5 Security (includes full XDR workloads) ~$12.00 USD (add-on to E3) E5 Security bundle
Microsoft Defender XDR (standalone) ~$57.50 USD per user/month (full E5 equivalent) Bundled in M365 E5
Defender Vulnerability Management add-on ~$2.00 USD per user/month Add-on to Plan 1 or Plan 2
Defender for Servers Plan 1 (Azure) ~$0.05 USD per server/hour Separate Azure billing
Defender for Servers Plan 2 (Azure) ~$0.02 USD per server/hour (if M365 E5 licensed) Separate Azure billing

Real talk on pricing: these are list prices. Enterprise Agreement customers negotiate 20 to 40% off depending on seat count and commitment length, almost without exception. The more useful question for most mid-market orgs isn’t “what does Plan 2 cost standalone” but “what’s the actual delta between our current E3 spend and what E5 Security adds.” For organizations already on E3, the E5 Security add-on at around $12 per user per month typically gets you Plan 2, Defender for Office 365 Plan 2, Defender for Identity, and Cloud App Security in one shot. That bundle math usually beats assembling the same coverage from individual SKUs.

We’ve seen organizations buy standalone Plan 2 licenses, get the endpoint EDR they wanted, and then discover they still had to purchase Defender for Identity separately to get the identity-based detections they assumed were included. That’s an expensive misread. Do the bundle math with your reseller before you sign anything.

Vulnerability management: the part most teams underestimate

Microsoft Defender Vulnerability Management, the standalone product as distinct from the TVM features inside Plan 2, has matured quite a bit between 2023 and 2026. It now covers software end-of-life tracking, security baseline comparisons, and browser extension risk scoring. That puts it in direct competition with Tenable.io and Qualys VMDR for organizations that don’t want another vendor contract sitting next to their Microsoft stack.

According to Microsoft’s own telemetry published in the Microsoft Digital Defense Report 2024, over 80% of successful ransomware attacks involved at least one unpatched known vulnerability. That stat should make every CISO look hard at whether their current vulnerability discovery cadence is actually weekly or whether it’s, honestly, “we run a scan once a month and hope for the best.” A lot of programs are the latter.

The add-on’s authenticated scan for network devices, routers, switches, firewalls, is genuinely useful for organizations that aren’t running a dedicated network vulnerability scanner. Not a replacement for something like Nessus in a mature program, but for SMB and mid-market it might cover enough ground to reduce tool sprawl meaningfully.

One practical caveat though: the remediation workflow inside Defender Vulnerability Management integrates cleanly with Microsoft Intune and Configuration Manager. If your patch management runs outside the Microsoft stack, say Ivanti or Tanium, you’re exporting tickets manually or via API. It works. It’s just not turnkey, and anyone who tells you otherwise is oversimplifying.

Which tier does your organization actually need?

Blunt answer: if you’re running more than 200 seats without EDR, you’re underprotected. Plan 1 is defensible for very small environments where someone is actively watching alerts from another source, but the absence of behavioral detection and incident timelines means you’re flying partially blind on anything beyond commodity malware.

Here’s how we’d actually work through this decision:

  • Under 300 seats, mostly on Microsoft 365 Business Premium already: you have Plan 1 bundled. Whether you need EDR depends on your industry threat profile. Healthcare, finance, legal, go to Plan 2 or the E5 Security add-on without much debate. For everyone else, at minimum document the risk decision so it’s not something that surfaces after an incident.
  • 300 to 2000 seats on E3: the E5 Security add-on is almost always better value than buying Plan 2 standalone, because you pick up identity and email coverage in the same motion. Do the bundle math with your reseller before committing to any standalone SKUs. Seriously, run the numbers first.
  • 2000-plus seats with a functioning SOC: you almost certainly need the full XDR suite. Gartner’s 2024 Market Guide for XDR found that unified alert correlation reduces mean time to respond by an average of 48% compared to operating siloed tools (see Gartner research on XDR, subscription required). That’s not a trivial number when you’re paying for analyst time.
  • Server workloads, regardless of which endpoint plan you pick: servers need Defender for Servers through Microsoft Defender for Cloud. Your endpoint license does not cover them. This is a gap that gets exploited, and it’s also a gap that surprises a lot of teams at audit time.

Automated Investigation and Response in Plan 2 deserves a specific warning. AIR is powerful, but it needs tuning before you trust it. Out of the box, in environments with custom tooling or legacy software, the false positive rate on automated remediation can create serious operational noise. We’ve watched AIR quarantine a critical line-of-business application on day three of a deployment because of unsigned executables. Build in a testing phase. Don’t put AIR in full remediation mode until you’ve observed its behavior in your specific environment for at least a few weeks.

FAQ

Can I use Microsoft Defender for Endpoint Plan 1 as my only endpoint security product?

Technically yes. Practically, it depends on your risk tolerance and what industry you’re in. Plan 1 covers next-gen antivirus, attack surface reduction, and device-based policies, which handles commodity threats reasonably well. What it completely lacks is any visibility into post-breach activity. If an attacker gets past the prevention layer, you have no EDR telemetry, no device timeline, no automated response. Nothing. For regulated industries or any org with genuinely sensitive data, Plan 1 alone is not an adequate control. You could pair it with Microsoft Sentinel ingesting whatever logs you can pull, but that adds real complexity and cost, and you’re still working with less data than Plan 2 gives you natively.

Is Microsoft Defender XDR pricing worth it compared to buying Plan 2 standalone?

Usually yes, once you hit a certain scale. Defender XDR is essentially the E5 security bundle, and per-seat the bundle almost always beats assembling the same coverage from standalone SKUs. The less obvious value is the cross-workload incident correlation. If you have separate tools for email and identity security alongside your endpoint coverage, you’re managing three alert queues instead of one. That operational cost is real, even if it doesn’t appear on a licensing invoice. The one case where the math might flip: if you have existing long-term contracts with third-party email or identity security vendors, breaking those early could wipe out the licensing savings entirely.

Does Microsoft Defender Vulnerability Management replace a dedicated scanner like Tenable or Qualys?

For some organizations, yes, it can. For mature programs with complex environments, probably not entirely. The Defender Vulnerability Management add-on handles agent-based discovery well for Windows and Linux endpoints managed through Intune or MECM, and network device scanning has improved. But there are real gaps: OT and ICS environments are not well covered, web application scanning is absent, and the reporting flexibility is still behind dedicated platforms. If your Tenable or Qualys contract renewal is coming up, it’s worth doing an honest feature gap analysis before you sign again. You might find the Microsoft tooling covers enough of your use cases to consolidate, depending on what you’re actually scanning.
